content: The empirical treatment of anti-Toxoplasma therapy in patients with AIDS and cerebral Chagas disease has been explored through case reports, literature reviews, and the development of diagnostic and therapeutic algorithms. Di Lorenzo et al. (1996) described findings from computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging in cases of Chagasic granulomatous encephalitis in immunosuppressed patients. Freilij et al. (1995) highlighted the coexistence of perinatal HIV infection and congenital Chagas disease. Pimentel et al. (1996) reported a case of Trypanosoma cruzi meningoencephalitis in an AIDS patient, which mimicked cerebral metastases. Sartori et al. (1995) documented the simultaneous occurrence of acute myocarditis and reactivated Chagas disease in an AIDS patient. Robinson (1995) reviewed parasitic infections associated with HIV/AIDS in the Caribbean, while Pittella (1993) provided an update on central nervous system involvement in Chagas disease. Rocha et al. (1994) examined the pathology of Chagas disease in patients with AIDS, and Nishioka et al. (1993) reported successful treatment of Chagas disease reactivation with benznidazole in an AIDS patient. Lages-Silva et al. (2002) described a case of Chagasic meningoencephalitis in an AIDS patient, including diagnosis, follow-up, and genetic characterization of Trypanosoma cruzi. Ferreira and Borges (2002) reviewed protozoan infections in immunocompromised patients. Sartori et al. (2002) noted an exacerbation of HIV viral load concurrent with asymptomatic reactivation of chronic Chagas disease. Antunes et al. (2002) discussed cerebral trypanosomiasis in AIDS patients. Harms and Feldmeier (2002) explored the bidirectional interactions between HIV infection and tropical parasitic diseases. Corti et al. (2000) identified Chagas disease as a cause of cerebral mass lesions in AIDS patients. Cahn et al. (2000) reviewed the epidemiology of AIDS in Latin America, while Concetti et al. (2000) reported a case of Chagas disease affecting the uterine cervix in an AIDS patient. Silva et al. (1999) described Trypanosoma cruzi meningoencephalitis in HIV-infected patients, and Dos Santos et al. (1999) reported ocular myositis and diffuse meningoencephalitis caused by Trypanosoma cruzi in an AIDS patient. Sartori et al. (1999) documented skin lesions as a manifestation of Chagas disease reactivation in an AIDS patient. Pagano et al. (1999) described tumor-like cerebral American trypanosomiasis in AIDS patients. Galhardo et al. (1999) reported reactivation of Trypanosoma cruzi infection in AIDS patients in Brazil. Sartori et al. (2002) compared parasitemia levels in chronic Chagas disease between HIV-positive and HIV-negative patients. Perez-Ramirez et al. (1999) analyzed clinical outcomes and parasite genetic diversity in HIV/Chagas co-infections. Brito et al. (2003) conducted genetic analyses of Trypanosoma cruzi strains under experimental immunosuppression. Revera et al. (2004) reported cardiac Chagas disease reactivation in AIDS patients. Valerga et al. (2005) described multifocal encephalitis in an AIDS patient. Picco (2005) emphasized the importance of considering Chagas disease as a co-infection in AIDS patients. Burgos et al. (2005) used molecular techniques to diagnose and type Trypanosoma cruzi populations in cerebral Chagas disease in AIDS patients. Cordova et al. (2008) reviewed cases of Chagas disease reactivation with central nervous system involvement in HIV-infected patients in Argentina. Rodriguez Guardado et al. (2011) highlighted the importance of screening for Chagas disease in HIV-positive immigrants from endemic areas. Almeida et al. (2010) examined the prevalence, clinical presentation, and natural history of Chagas/HIV co-infection in patients without effective antiretroviral therapy. Lopez (2010) reported a case of Chagasic meningoencephalitis in an HIV/AIDS patient with three years of survival. Warley et al. (2010) discussed the development of AIDS-defining infections and neoplasms after initiating highly effective antiretroviral therapy. Almeida et al. (2009) described diagnostic challenges in distinguishing between acute myocarditis and chronic Chagasic cardiomyopathy in Chagas/AIDS co-infection. De Almeida et al. (2009) evaluated the use of itraconazole or ketoconazole for etiological treatment in Trypanosoma cruzi/HIV co-infection. Burgos et al. (2008) identified a central nervous system tropism of Trypanosoma cruzi I in Chagas reactivation due to AIDS. Sica et al. (2008) described tumor-like Chagasic encephalitis in AIDS patients. Verdú et al. (2009) provided evidence of Chagas disease reactivation with central nervous system involvement through peripheral blood smear analysis. Bisio et al. (2013) reported successful benznidazole treatment of Chagasic encephalitis in a pregnant woman with AIDS. Solari et al. (1993) documented successful treatment of Trypanosoma cruzi encephalitis in a patient with hemophilia and AIDS. Rocha et al. (1993) described meningoencephalitis and myocarditis caused by Trypanosoma cruzi in an AIDS patient. Metze and Maciel (1993) reviewed the relationship between AIDS and Chagas disease. Oddó et al. (1992) reported acute Chagas disease in AIDS patients. Gluckstein et al. (1992) identified Chagas disease as a cause of cerebral mass lesions in AIDS patients. Rosemberg et al. (1992) described fatal meningoencephalitis caused by Trypanosoma cruzi reactivation in an AIDS patient. Gallo et al. (1992) reported acute central nervous system infection by Trypanosoma cruzi in AIDS patients. Ferreira et al. (1991) documented acute fatal Trypanosoma cruzi meningoencephalitis in an HIV-positive hemophiliac patient. Torrealba et al. (1990) emphasized the value of brain biopsy in AIDS patients with cerebral mass lesions. Livramento et al. (1989) analyzed cerebrospinal fluid abnormalities in AIDS patients. The guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of Chagas disease include recommendations for antiparasitic therapy, with benznidazole and nifurtimox as the primary options. The importance of comprehensive evaluation and formal prescription by attending physicians is emphasized for children and patients with chronic infections.
